title: Research Paradigms and Western Philosophers
summary: What a paradigm is; the Kuhn cycle (pre-science → normal science → model drift → model crisis → model revolution → paradigm shift); paradigm elements (ontology, epistemology, methodology, axiology); major paradigms (positivism, post-positivism, constructivism, interpretivism, pragmatism, critical); and Western philosophers from Descartes to Popper.

notes.t: A paradigm is a fundamental framework or worldview that guides research and knowledge development in a field. In psychology, paradigms influence theories, research approaches and interpretations of human behaviour.

r: No established framework; multiple conflicting explanations exist for a phenomenon.
A dominant paradigm emerges; researchers work within this framework, solving puzzles using existing theories.
Anomalies accumulate and begin to challenge the existing paradigm.
Confidence in the current paradigm weakens; scientists search for new explanations.
Competing theories emerge and one gains wider acceptance.
The new paradigm replaces the old, becoming the foundation for future research.

notes.t: The cycle may restart when new anomalies arise. Psychology's own history moves through these stages: the soul/mind era was pre-science, Wundt's lab began normal science, and the cognitive revolution was a paradigm shift.

r: The nature of reality — what exists and what can be known.
The nature of knowledge — how we acquire and justify knowledge.
The approach used to study reality, including research methods.
The role of values and ethics in research and knowledge.

notes.t: Two main ontological perspectives: realism (reality exists independently of human perception) and relativism (reality is subjective and varies based on human perception and interpretation). Epistemology deals with objective knowledge (independent of personal beliefs) versus subjective knowledge (created through social interactions and experiences).

r: Naïve realism — reality is objective and knowable
Critical realism — single reality but imperfectly known
John Dewey, William James, Harvey Carr
Relativism — reality is dynamic and practical
Relativism — shaped by social, historical, political contexts

notes.t: Positivism, introduced by Auguste Comte, emphasises empirical knowledge based on positive, real facts rather than speculation or intuition. It follows naïve realism, believing our understanding of reality is 100% accurate. Post-positivism emerged as a response to positivism's limitations, based on critical realism — knowledge is objective but complete certainty is not assumed.

r: Mind–body dualism; 'Cogito, ergo sum'; animal spirits; reflex mechanism; interactionism at the pineal gland
Inductive reasoning; scientific method; observation; rejection of innate ideas

notes.t: Karl Popper held that a theory is scientific only if it can be tested and potentially proven false (falsifiability); the more a theory exposes itself to refutation, the stronger it is.

Falsifiability means a theory must be disprovable, not verifiable beyond doubt. Interpretivism does not seek absolute truths but subjective understanding. Popper's falsifiability is a frequently tested distinction.
